titleStmt.title: Cognitive Neuroscience Tools in Economic Experiments Investigating the Decision Making Process
titleStmt.author: Anna Borawska

bibl.title: Cognitive Neuroscience Tools in Economic Experiments Investigating the Decision Making Process

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: The proposed analysis could allow for the better design of economic experiments conducted with the use of the most up-to date technology available.

span.label: decision making process in economic experiments
span.quote: Investigating the neurophysiological signals of experiment participants can give researchers a deeper insight into a decision making process.

span.label: review
span.quote: The research was conducted with the use of literature review method, according to a procedure consisting of five main stages:

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: measuring neurophysiological activity bypasses the self-report distortions (demand characteristics, participants' limited insight) that mask the true mechanisms of choice
span.quote: By measuring the neurophysiological activity of the subjects, researchers hope to bypass such problems as a lack of insight into the true mechanisms of choice (Ariely, Berns, 2010).

span.label: The review deliberately covers only recent contributions, restricting the literature searched to the previous ten years.
span.quote: In the scope of neuroscientific research and experimental economics, only the newest contributions were chosen (published in the past 10 years).

span.label: Only three of the decision-process phases are considered; the implementation phase is excluded as not a mental task.
span.quote: The rest of the article will be therefore focused on three stages only: Intelligent, Design and Choice.

span.label: The equipment's recording requirements confine the research mostly to individual humans.
span.note: what this limits: the topic distribution of neuroeconomic experiments as reflecting what matters most: the paper attributes the restriction to individual humans to the recording method and the equipment needed, and lists the resulting dominant trends immediately after
span.quote: However, due to the specific way of recording the data and the equipment that is needed, the performed research is limited mostly to the issues of individual human beings.

span.label: brain and body measurement techniques (fMRI, EEG, fNIRS, galvanic skin response, heart rate, eye-tracking) are taken over into the design of economic experiments on decision making
span.quote: The aim of the article is to show how neuroscience techniques can contribute to economic experiments, especially those concerning decision making.

span.label: decision making process
span.quote: A general decision-making process proposed by Simon (1960, 1977) involves three main phases: Intelligence, Design, and Choice.

span.label: Intelligence
span.quote: Intelligence (identification) activity involves gathering and processing information, providing cues for recognizing potential decision needs or opportunities (diagnosis), and for formulating alternatives.

span.label: Identification
span.quote: propose slightly different terms to name these stages: Identification, Development and Selection.

span.label: decision-making phases - Simon's naming: Intelligence, Design and Choice
span.quote: A general decision-making process proposed by Simon (1960, 1977) involves three main phases: Intelligence, Design, and Choice.

span.label: decision-making phases - the same three stages under a different naming convention: Identification, Development and Selection
span.quote: propose slightly different terms to name these stages: Identification, Development and Selection. Despite the differences in naming convention, these three following stages of the decision making process consist of very similar activities.

span.label: builds-on → Simon's (1960, 1977) three-phase model of the decision-making process
span.quote: A general decision-making process proposed by Simon (1960, 1977) involves three main phases: Intelligence, Design, and Choice.

span.label: Intelligence —renamed-across-fields→ Identification
span.quote: A general decision-making process proposed by Simon (1960, 1977) involves three main phases: Intelligence, Design, and Choice. Other authors, like Mintzberg, Raisinghani and Theoret (1976), propose slightly different terms to name these stages: Identification, Development and Selection. Despite the differences in naming convention, these three following stages of the decision making process consist of very similar activities.

span.label: Because of the way neurophysiological data must be recorded and the equipment required, neuroscience-based economic experiments are confined mostly to questions about individual human beings rather than groups or markets.
span.quote: However, due to the specific way of recording the data and the equipment that is needed, the performed research is limited mostly to the issues of individual human beings.

span.label: EEG's very good temporal resolution makes it the tool of choice for tracking how brain activity changes over time and for analysing reactions to external stimuli.
span.quote: Because of its very good temporal resolution, this method is usually used to study changes in brain activity in time and to analyse reactions to external stimuli (Zaleśkiewicz, 2008).

span.label: fMRI localises activity by showing how much oxygen is delivered to specific parts of the brain, which is what EEG cannot do.
span.quote: In such applications, fMRI is much better suited. With its help, you can tell how much oxygen is delivered to specific parts of the brain and deduce their activity.

span.label: fMRI buys very good spatial resolution at the price of an examination procedure that is cumbersome for the participant.
span.quote: Functional magnetic resonance imaging has very good spatial resolution but conducting an examination with the use of this method can be cumbersome.

span.label: Neurophysiological measurement can be more faithful to what participants actually do than self-report measures are.
span.quote: First, they may offer greater fidelity than measures relying upon self-report.

span.label: Substantial information processing in the brain that drives economic decisions cannot be observed at all through behavioural research methods.
span.quote: Secondly, there are substantial information processes in the brain that determine economic decision making that are not easily observed through behavioural research methods.

span.label: Experiments using transmagnetic stimulation establish a causal relationship between brain activity and economic choice that is independent of environmental factors.
span.quote: These studies confirm a causal relationship between brain activity and economic choice, above and beyond environmental factors.

span.label: Neuroscience techniques can surface fundamental principles of decision making - such as the effect of physical environment, mood or cultural background - that traditional economic research treated as irrelevant.
span.quote: They may reveal fundamental principles of decision making that may not have been considered relevant in traditional economic research.

span.label: Every later model of the decision process still contains Simon's three phases of intelligence, design and choice, differing only in naming and in how finely the phases are split.
span.quote: However, the three main phases proposed by Simon are always present (although sometimes with slightly diff erent names), and all existent models are in many respects similar (Fredrickson, 1985; Gore et al., 1992; Schwenk, 1984).

span.label: Behavioural experiments can document that people deviate from expected utility theory, but only cognitive neuroscience can supply the explanation of why they are not as rational as the theory assumes.
span.quote: Experimental economics has an insight into some deviations from the EU theory on the basis of behavioural evidence given by the participants of research but only with cognitive neuroscience would it be possible to find some explanations why people do not behave as rationally as they are supposed to.

span.label: Both the decision-making and the cognitive neuroscience literatures have concentrated on the final phase of the process - evaluation and choice - leaving the intelligence and design phases comparatively unstudied.
span.quote: The existing decision-making literature in general, and the cognitive neuroscience literature in particular, has focused especially on the last phase of the decision making process: evaluation and choice (Fellows, 2004) and this aspect has been the most intensively studied to date.

span.label: The cost of the specialised equipment, fMRI above all, is one of the practical obstacles to using neuroscience in economic experiments.
span.quote: Another drawback is the cost connected with using the specialised equipment, especially when it comes to fMRI.

span.label: A single cognitive neuroscience experiment yields an enormous amount of neurophysiological data, which forces the use of very sophisticated analysis methods.
span.quote: Last but not least, the amount of neurophysiological data that is obtained during the average cognitive neuroscience experiment is enormous, thus demanding very sophisticated data analysis methods.

span.label: decision-making process (decision process)
span.quote: Generally speaking, a decision-making process (simply called a decision process) begins with the awareness of a decision problem, and ends up with a final solution among finite or infinite alternatives.

span.label: neuroimaging
span.quote: Neuroimaging is associated with a group of research methods used to studying the structure and function of the brain.

span.label: electroencephalography (EEG)
span.quote: EEG is focused on the measurement of brain electrical activity recorded by electrodes placed on the scalp at specific locations (Purves et al., 2013).

span.label: functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS)
span.quote: there is another one, quite novel imaging method, i.e. functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) – a non-invasive technique for the optical estimation of cortical activity

span.label: neurophysiological techniques
span.quote: Neurophysiological techniques are based on the correlation of brain functions with physiological sensations (Zaleśkiewicz, 2008).

span.label: galvanic skin-response (GSR) measurement
span.quote: The GSR measurement is based on detecting electrical changes in the skin (Dawson, Schell, Filion, 2007) and it is mostly performed on the skin of the hand (fingers).

span.label: eye-tracking (ET)
span.quote: Eye-tracking, on the other hand, is an effective tool for experimental research because of its abilities to detect the eye position, gaze direction, sequence of eye movement and visual adaptation during cognitive activities.

span.label: 650–1000 nm — the infrared wavelength window whose low absorption by biological tissue fNIRS exploits to estimate cortical activity
span.quote: It relies on the low optical absorption of the biological tissue of the infrared radiation in the 650–1000 nm wavelength window (Ferrari, Quaresima, 2012).
